items.title: Major volcanic eruptions inject ash into the stratosphere
items.claim: How high can a large eruption column reach?

options.text: Up to 5 km — high but contained in the troposphere
Plinian eruptions can exceed 30-40 km, well into the stratosphere — Mount Pinatubo (1991) reached around 35 km
Only the visible smoke is observable
No eruption has reached the stratosphere in recorded history

items.reveal:
Plinian eruptions (named after Pliny the Younger's description of Vesuvius in 79 CE) drive ash and sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, where they can spread globally and remain for years. Pinatubo (June 1991) cooled global temperatures by around 0.5°C for 18 months.

Tambora (1815, VEI 7) caused the 'Year Without a Summer' (1816) — crop failures across Europe and North America, snow in June. Krakatoa (1883, VEI 6) produced spectacular sunsets globally. Toba (around 74,000 years ago, VEI 8) may have caused a population bottleneck in early humans.
items.why: Volcanic forcing is one of the strongest natural climate drivers on year-to-decade scales. Climate models calibrate against these events because the signal is large and well-dated.

items.title: Tropical cyclones need 26.5 °C sea surface temperatures
items.claim: What conditions are required for tropical cyclone formation?

options.text: Sea surface temperatures of at least around 26.5 °C, low vertical wind shear, sufficient distance from the equator (Coriolis force) and a pre-existing disturbance — typically 5-30° latitude

items.reveal:
Energy source: latent heat released as water vapour condenses. Tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator (insufficient Coriolis force to spin) and weaken rapidly over land or cool water.

Naming conventions: Atlantic/East Pacific = hurricanes; Northwest Pacific = typhoons; South Pacific/Indian Ocean = cyclones. Same phenomenon. The Saffir-Simpson scale (Category 1-5) classifies Atlantic and East Pacific storms by sustained wind speed.

Storm surge — wind-driven raising of sea level along the coast — is usually the deadliest hazard (Hurricane Katrina, 2005; Cyclone Bhola, 1970, killed at least 300,000 in East Pakistan).
items.why: Climate change is raising sea surface temperatures and expanding the zone where tropical cyclones can form and intensify. The deadliest hazard is also rising as warmer air holds more moisture.

items.title: Antarctica is governed by an international treaty

options.text: It is divided into national territories
The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze territorial claims, demilitarised the continent and committed it to scientific cooperation; 56 countries are now parties
It is divided between Argentina and Chile

items.reveal:
The original 12 signatories (1959) included the US, USSR, UK, Australia, France, Argentina and Chile. The treaty entered force in 1961. The Protocol on Environmental Protection (Madrid Protocol, 1991, in force 1998) prohibits mineral extraction.

Seven countries maintain dormant territorial claims (UK, Norway, France, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, Chile). The US and Russia reserve the right to claim. Treaty parties operate around 70 year-round research stations.

The treaty is one of the most successful international agreements of the Cold War era — both superpowers wanted the demilitarisation to apply to the other.
items.why: Some territory remains explicitly outside the state system. Antarctica's governance shows what's possible when no major power has a strong sovereignty claim — but also illustrates how fragile such arrangements may be as resource interests grow.
